procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated July 27, 1964 of the Patna High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 481 of 1963, dismissing Jamuna Singh's appeal and confirming his conviction and sentence under ss. 323 and 436 read with s. 109, I. P. C.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Four convicted persons (including Jamuna Singh and Jodha Singh) appealed to the Patna High Court. The High Court acquitted two of the appellants. It acquitted Jodha Singh of the offence under s. 436 I.P.C. but maintained his conviction under s. 323 I.P.C. Jamuna Singh's appeal was dismissed.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Jamuna Singh appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the Patna High Court's decision to dismiss his appeal and uphold his conviction.

decision.conviction_status: The appeal against the conviction under s. 323 I.P.C. is dismissed. The conviction under s. 436 read with s. 109 I.P.C. is altered to one under s. 436 read with s. 115 I.P.C.
decision.sentence_status: Reduced to four years' rigorous imprisonment.

issue.issue_text: Whether a person can be convicted of abetting an offence when the person alleged to have committed that offence in consequence of the abetment has been acquitted.

law.name: Section 107, Indian Penal Code (I.P.C.)
law.description: Defines abetment as occurring in one of three ways: instigating a person, engaging in a conspiracy, or intentionally aiding the doing of an act.

law.name: Section 108, Explanation 2, I.P.C.
law.description: Clarifies that to constitute the offence of abetment, it is not necessary that the act abetted should actually be committed.

law.name: Sections 115 & 116, I.P.C.
law.description: Provide for the punishment of abetment even if the offence abetted is not committed.

application.description: The Court first established that there is no absolute rule in law that an abettor cannot be convicted if the principal offender is acquitted. The outcome depends on the specific nature and manner of the abetment.
The Court analyzed the three types of abetment under Section 107 I.P.C.: instigation, conspiracy, and intentional aiding.

For abetment by 'instigation' or 'conspiracy', the Court found that the offence of abetment is complete at the moment the person instigates another or engages in the conspiracy. It does not require the main offence to be committed. This is supported by Section 108, Explanation 2. Therefore, the acquittal of the person who was instigated or conspired with does not prevent the conviction of the abettor.

However, the Court made a crucial distinction for the third type of abetment: 'intentionally aiding'. In this specific case, the charge of abetment against a person is expected to fail if the person they allegedly aided is acquitted. The logic is that if the principal offender is found not to have committed the offence, then the accused abettor cannot be guilty of having 'aided' them in committing it.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a person can be convicted of abetting an offence even when the principal offender has been acquitted, specifically in cases where the abetment was by 'instigation' or 'conspiracy'. However, if the abetment was by 'intentionally aiding' the commission of the offence, the abettor's conviction is expected to fail upon the acquittal of the principal offender.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant could be held guilty under s. 436 read with s. 109 I.P.C. when the person charged with the main offence under s. 436 had been acquitted and there was no finding that the fire was set by any other person at the appellant's instigation.

facts: The appellant was charged with abetting an offence under s. 436 of the Indian Penal Code (I.P.C.), which is mischief by fire.
Specifically, the appellant was accused of instigating his co-accused, Jodha Singh, to set fire to a hut.
The trial court convicted Jodha Singh for the main offence (s. 436) and the appellant for abetting it (s. 436 read with s. 109).
However, the High Court acquitted Jodha Singh, finding him not guilty of setting the fire.
Despite acquitting the main offender, the High Court upheld the appellant's conviction for abetment.
The appellant argued that his conviction for abetment was illegal since the person he allegedly instigated had been acquitted.
law: The Court distinguished between two types of abetment under the I.P.C.
Section 109 I.P.C. applies when an offence is committed *in consequence of* the abetment.
Section 115 I.P.C. applies when a person abets an offence punishable with life imprisonment, but the offence is *not committed* as a result of the abetment.
The Court affirmed the principle that an abettor can be convicted even if the main offender is acquitted. The abettor's guilt depends on the act of abetment itself (e.g., instigation).
application: The Court found that the High Court had established the fact that the appellant did instigate Jodha Singh to set the hut on fire. This act of instigation constituted the offence of abetment.
However, since Jodha Singh was acquitted, the law presumes that the main offence (setting the fire) was not committed by him in consequence of the appellant's instigation.
Therefore, the condition for a conviction under s. 109 I.P.C. was not met.
Because the appellant's act of instigation was proven, but the instigated offence was not committed by the person instigated, the appellant was guilty under s. 115 I.P.C. instead.
The Court noted that while the hut was burned by someone, there was no finding that this other person acted on the appellant's instigation, which is necessary to sustain a charge under s. 109.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the appellant could not be held guilty under s. 436 read with s. 109 I.P.C. because the person he instigated was acquitted, meaning the offence was not committed in consequence of the abetment. However, since the act of instigation itself was proven, the Court altered the conviction to the lesser offence of s. 436 read with s. 115 I.P.C. and reduced the sentence accordingly.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a person can be convicted of abetting an offence when the person alleged to have committed that offence in consequence of the abetment has been acquitted.
appellant_arguments: The conviction for abetment (s. 436 read with s. 109 I.P.C.) is bad in law when the person alleged to have committed the main offence at the abettor's instigation (Jodha Singh) has been acquitted of that offence.

Citing a similar case, it was argued that if the principal offender is acquitted and the main offence is held not to have been committed, then no question of intentionally aiding the commission of that offence can arise.
respondent_arguments: The High Court had already held that the appellant had instigated his co-accused to commit the offence under s. 436 I.P.C.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant could be held guilty under s. 436 read with s. 109 I.P.C. when the person charged with the main offence under s. 436 had been acquitted and there was no finding that the fire was set by any other person at the appellant's instigation.
appellant_arguments: The appellant could not be held guilty under s. 436 read with s. 109 because the person charged with the main offence was acquitted, and there was no finding by the courts that the fire was set by any other person who was participating in the incident at the appellant's instigation.
respondent_arguments: The High Court's finding that the appellant had instigated his co-accused to commit the offence was sufficient to uphold the conviction under s. 436 read with s. 109 I.P.C.

cases.case_name: Barendra Kumar Ghosh v. The King Emperor
cases.principle: Relied on for the legal position regarding the conviction of an abettor when the principal offender is acquitted.

cases.case_name: Faguna Kanta Nath v. The State of Assam
cases.principle: Relied on for the legal position regarding the conviction of an abettor when the principal offender is acquitted.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A conviction for abetment under Section 109 of the Indian Penal Code is not legally sustainable without a finding that the principal offense was committed by a person as a consequence of the abetment. The acquittal of the person charged with the main offense, coupled with a lack of finding that anyone else committed the act due to the instigation, invalidates a conviction under this section.
obiter: It is, we think, too unreal to hold that the person who set fire to the hut of Mst. Rasmani did so irrespective, or independently, of the order given by the present appellant.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The appellant could not be held guilty for abetment under s. 436 read with s. 109 I.P.C. because the person charged with the main offence was acquitted and there was no finding by the lower courts that the fire was set by any other person at the appellant's instigation. However, since the High Court had established as a fact that the appellant had instigated his co-accused to commit the offence, he is guilty of abetment under s. 436 read with s. 115 I.P.C., which applies when an offence is abetted but not committed.
legal_tests_applied: For a conviction under s. 109 I.P.C. (abetment where the act is committed), it is necessary that the main offence was actually committed by someone in consequence of the abetment. If the named principal offender is acquitted, there must be a finding that some other person committed the act.
The act of abetment (e.g., by instigation) is a substantive offence in itself, distinct from the principal offence.
If an offence is abetted but is not committed in consequence of the abetment, the abettor is punishable under s. 115 I.P.C.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant lost his appeal against being convicted for abetment because the High Court's finding of fact that he 'had instigated his co-accused to commit the offence under s. 436 I.P.C.' was not overturned. This act of instigation is sufficient to constitute the crime of abetment, irrespective of whether the instigated offence was ultimately committed.
why_respondent_won: The respondent succeeded in maintaining a conviction for abetment because the court accepted the High Court's factual finding that the appellant had instigated the crime. While this was insufficient for a conviction under s. 109 I.P.C. due to the acquittal of the principal and lack of other findings, it was sufficient to prove the offence of abetment for which the punishment is prescribed under s. 115 I.P.C.
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning reinforces the legal policy that instigating a serious crime is itself a punishable wrong, regardless of the outcome. The law punishes the act of abetment to deter individuals from encouraging or aiding the commission of offences, even if their efforts do not ultimately succeed.
